meera_replies: Grandfather told me the temple sweeper knew every room. Even when a door was shut, someone had to tell her where to stop sweeping.
A weaver once gave her daughter a length of plain cloth. The girl knew her mother’s hand by the one thread in each row that caught the morning light.
When I was small, a clerk promised Grandfather one name from his ledger. By dusk the clerk was still reading. Grandfather always did know how to ask a question.

aftermath.1:
Then you see the login log. The professor's account logged in at 3:12 am. Six hours after he was found dead.

Someone is wearing a dead man's identity.
aftermath.2:
As you read it, your phone lights up. The portal shows a new login from the professor's account. Right now. While you are logged in.

He is in the system with you.
aftermath.3: The reader list holds three names: Vasudevan Namboothiri, a priest who died of a snakebite in 1974; Lakshmikutty Amma, an archives librarian who died after a fall in 2009; and Professor Raghavan Menon, found dead in 2026. A donor note from Kunnathu Charitable Trust bars MS-1794-047 from digitisation or display. The line marked "Current reader" carries your name. The archive has written you into its history.
aftermath.4:
The 1974 letter is from priest Vasudevan Namboothiri. He writes that hereditary trustee Sankaran Namboothiri was murdered and the deed forged; he fears the Kunnathu family. Days later, Vasudevan dies of a snakebite.

The police memo records Meera found dead at home, apparent suicide. You know her for three days. You know that word is wrong.

Three hours after the police find her, your phone lights with Meera's name. Two words:

"stop reading."
aftermath.5:
Kunjiraman, accountant at the Vadakkumkara temple, writes what happened in 1794. On the night of the new moon, the Kunnathu men murder hereditary trustee Sankaran Namboothiri and leave him in the temple pond. The record calls it a drowning. By morning, a deed bearing Sankaran's signature gives the temple's 140 acres of paddy fields to the family. Kunjiraman sees the deed written; the hand is not Sankaran's. The family's wealth rests on that theft.

Two hundred and thirty years later, Devan Kunnathu is preparing a township on the same land.
aftermath.6:
The emails are blunt. "The professor is getting close to the manuscript. Arrange an accident. Five lakh, same as before." "Done. Heart attack, like the others. Make sure the manuscript never reaches the public site." "The girl is asking questions. Handle it."

The attachment has no words: a photograph of you, taken from outside your window the night before. He has been watching every page, every login, every chapter. He knew your name before you knew his.

You look outside. Rain dims the empty street. The car with its lights off is gone.

evidence.first_leaf_note: If you are reading this, I am dead. It is not a curse. It is a man. He knows you are reading this. Do not trust anyone who offers to help you. — R.M.
evidence.priest_letter: I have read one page of the grandham. It says the trustee was murdered and the deed forged. I am afraid. If something happens to me, look at the Kunnathu family. The key to the middle leaves is the name of the goddess. She will open what men have locked.
evidence.confession: I, Kunjiraman, accountant of this temple, write this in cipher so that it may outlive me. On the night of the new moon, the Kunnathu men came for the trustee Sankaran Namboothiri and left him in the temple pond. By morning they had a deed, signed in his hand, giving the temple's fields to their family. I saw the deed written. The hand was not his. I write this so that the truth outlives the men who buried it.
evidence.professor_note: Devan Kunnathu paid for my death. The manuscript is real. Meera, publish it. — R.M.
evidence.last_leaf: The fourth reader will finish what I started.
